planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall or early spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, sharply drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun and winter wind; Rebecca resents both waterlogging and prolonged drought, so consistent moisture without sogginess is essential while roots establish.

directions: Site Rebecca winter daphne in dappled or morning sun with afternoon shade, in rich, evenly moist, sharply drained soil, since standing water around the roots is the most common cause of sudden collapse in this genus. A sport of Daphne odora with the same intensely sweet, carrying fragrance, Rebecca is distinguished by broad, irregular deep-gold margins on its glossy evergreen leaves, giving the shrub ornamental interest even when not in bloom. Clusters of small, waxy, rose-pink to white flowers open from midwinter into early spring and perfume the air for many yards around on mild days, making it a prized choice near an entry, window, or path. In the Gulf South, give it the coolest, most sheltered partial-shade spot available and avoid heavy clay; established plants otherwise need only routine watering during dry spells and light shaping after bloom.

planting.note: Plant in spring or early fall in humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline, well-drained soil in partial shade; a sport of 'Eternal Fragrance' with the same repeat-blooming habit, Summer Ice adds a crisp white leaf margin that brightens shaded borders even between flushes of bloom.

directions: Grow Summer Ice in evenly moist, neutral to slightly alkaline, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from hot afternoon sun and drying wind. This compact, deciduous-leaning hybrid daphne carries crisp white margins on its blue-green foliage and blooms in repeated flushes from spring through fall rather than the single winter show typical of most daphnes, with clusters of pale pink, sweetly fragrant flowers opening intermittently all season. It performs reliably through USDA zone 8 but struggles with the sustained heat and humidity of zone 9 Gulf Coast summers, so gardeners there should treat it as a container or shaded microclimate specimen rather than a permanent border shrub. Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged, mulch to cool the roots, and deadhead spent flower clusters lightly to encourage the next flush.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall or spring in humus-rich, moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full to partial shade; Pontic daphne is native to shaded woodland understory in the Black Sea region and, unlike many daphnes, genuinely prefers deep shade over sun.

directions: Site Pontic daphne in full to dappled shade in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil, ideally beneath a light woodland canopy that mimics its native Black Sea forest understory. This low, rounded evergreen shrub carries glossy, narrow, dark-green leaves and, in spring, pairs of slender, spidery, yellow-green flowers held close to the stems that release a light, sweet fragrance most noticeable at close range or in the evening. Small black berries follow the flowers and are best kept away from children and pets, as with other Daphne species. It is one of the more shade-tolerant members of the genus and one of the easier daphnes to grow well in humid climates, provided drainage stays sharp and soil never dries out completely; water during dry spells and avoid disturbing the shallow root system once established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall or spring in gritty, humus-rich, sharply drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade; Daphne tangutica is a Chinese mountain species that tolerates more sun than Daphne pontica but still performs best out of hot afternoon exposure.

directions: Grow Tangut daphne in gritty, humus-rich soil with sharp drainage in partial shade, avoiding both hot midday sun and constantly wet ground. Native to scrub and forest margins in western China, it forms a dense, rounded evergreen mound of narrow, leathery, dark-green leaves and produces clusters of white flowers flushed purple-pink on the reverse in early spring, carrying the classic sweet daphne fragrance at close range. Small red berries follow the flowers and, as with all daphnes, are toxic if eaten. It is somewhat more tolerant of routine garden conditions than many daphne species, but still resents being moved once settled and benefits from a gravel mulch that keeps the crown dry while the roots stay cool and evenly moist. Prune only to remove dead or damaged wood, ideally right after flowering.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full shade; Itea japonica tolerates wetter soil than most shrubs and is a good choice for a shaded rain garden edge or streambank planting.

directions: Plant Japanese sweetspire in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade, where it thrives in conditions that would stress most other flowering shrubs. Native to woodland streambanks in Japan, it is closely related to the more familiar Itea virginica but carries longer, more pendulous racemes of small, fragrant white flowers in late spring to early summer, followed by good yellow to reddish fall color on its arching deciduous stems. It spreads slowly by suckers to form a loose colony over time, making it valuable for stabilizing shaded, damp slopes or the margins of a rain garden where standing water is occasional. Water deeply and regularly, especially during establishment and dry summer spells, and prune out the oldest canes after bloom to keep the colony open and vigorous.

common_name: Chinese Fragrant Sweet Box (Long-Leaf Ruscifolia Sarcococca)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; this Chinese botanical variety of Sarcococca ruscifolia is distinguished from the typical variety mainly by longer, narrower leaves and a slightly more open habit.

directions: Site in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, where this variety tolerates dry shade and root competition beneath established trees once settled. Sarcococca ruscifolia var. chinensis is a wild-collected Chinese botanical variety within the widely grown ruscifolia species, distinguished chiefly by its longer, more slender, glossy dark-green leaves and a somewhat taller, more upright and open habit than the typical variety, though selections such as 'Dragon Gate' have since been made from within this variety for a more compact, arching form. Small, inconspicuous cream-white flowers open in midwinter and produce the same powerfully sweet, honey-vanilla fragrance the genus is known for, followed by red berries that persist into summer. Water during dry spells while establishing; once rooted in, it needs little supplemental irrigation and requires pruning only to remove damaged or overly leggy stems.
